10965-the-world-turned-upside-down-or-no:
A small illustrated chapbook for children, this book turns the world upside down for laughs and learning. Each page pairs a plain fact with a strange reversal: seeing a butcher kill a hog is no news, but seeing a hare run after a dog is strange indeed. A tailor rides a goose, a rat builds a house, a dog plays the flute, and a lamb hunts a bear.

Roman and italic alphabets open the book, so children practise letters while enjoying the jokes. Pictures face the verses, showing cats fiddling while mice dance and horses playing chess. The chapbook belongs to early children's publishing, where nonsense taught reading and rewarded attention with surprise on every page.
11438-the-willows:
Algernon Blackwood's 1907 novella The Willows follows two travelers down the Danube between Vienna and Budapest. into a region of singular loneliness where the river spreads into marshes, painted Sümpfe on maps, covered by a vast sea of low willow bushes. The willows never become trees, remaining humble bushes swaying on slender stems, their silver leaves turning in wind waves like a sea. Channels, whirlpools, and foaming rapids tear at sandy banks.

Blackwood builds horror from landscape itself: the plain seems moving and alive, and the willows seem aware. The Willows is widely counted among the finest weird tales in English, influential and unsettling without monsters. Readers of supernatural fiction should start here for atmosphere over explanation.
13410-some-private-views:
James Payn gathers essays first printed in the Nineteenth Century and the Times, in a new edition of 1881 dedicated to Horace N. Pym. He writes on the midway inn, the critic on the hearth, sham admiration in literature, the pinch of poverty, story-telling, and penny fiction, then on hotels, maid-servants, men-servants, and whist players.

Payn claims his thoughts are not his own but the hidden common thought of all. A lady's hand crushed in a carriage door shows the pinch of poverty felt by birth and breeding, while Wilkie Collins's unknown public, readers by millions, waits to learn discrimination. The essays are chatty, observant, and mildly satirical about Victorian reading, service, and society.
14240-reviews:
Robert Ross edited this 1908 Methuen volume of Oscar Wilde's reviews, dedicating it to Mrs. Carew. Ross recalls eight years managing Wilde's literary property, with one friendship that annulled its disappointments. Dinners and Dishes opens the set, quoting Baudelaire: a man can live three days without bread but not one day without poetry. Pictures and music may lapse, Wilde insists, but poetry cannot.

Scottish and Australian letters fill the middle. Early Scots singers loved gardens, flowers, and birdsong, but not wild moorland, until Montgomerie wandered banks and braes and Drummond sang flood, forest, and hillside mist. Allan Ramsay, Thomson, and Beattie follow toward Wordsworth. Australian verse disappoints Wilde's reviewer: page after page of echoes without music, reflections without beauty, and magazine verse for colonial papers. Henry Clarence Kendall stands out as an exception. Criticism here stays witty, learned, and severe.
14282-a-merry-dialogue-declaringe-the-pr:
Desiderius Erasmus wrote this merry dialogue, printed in English in 1557, on shrewish wives and honest wives. Two women, Eulalia and Xantippa, talk over marriage, temper, and the art of living with a husband. Eulalia urges patience, good cheer, and a ready welcome at meeting. Xantippa answers with complaints of a beast of a husband. The text keeps the old spelling of its age, with its quaint forms and long sentences.

Eulalia holds that most husbands turn ill through their wives' own fault, and that a wife should never scold her man before company. She should speak her mind in private, then drop the matter and turn to pastime. Complaints, if they must be made, should go to his kin, not to strangers, and should blame the fault, not the man. The dialogue gives Tudor advice on wedlock: gentle rule, held tongues, and peace kept at home.
14531-the-singing-man-a-book-of-songs-an:
Josephine Preston Peabody's 1911 book of poems, published by Houghton Mifflin, gathers songs and shadows first printed in the Atlantic, Scribner's, and Harper's magazines. The contents run from The Singing Man to The Long Lane.

Peabody writes of trees, foundlings, feasters, golden shoes, and Paestum at noon, with a byway poem contrasting highway sun and byway despair. Her verse is lyrical and musical, with a touch of the Pre-Raphaelite. The collection shows a Boston poet of the early century at her most melodious, and it remains her best-known book.
14654-a-daughter-of-the-snows:
Jack London's A Daughter of the Snows, published in 1902 with illustrations by Frederick C. Yohn, follows Frona Welse in the Yukon gold rush. London had already written The Son of the Wolf and The Call of the Wild.

Frona arrives by steamer, hurrying because she was born in the big log-house between the pines and the river. She moves through a rough camp society of dances, waltzes, fur caps, and moose-skin moccasins. London makes her a strong, educated heroine who holds her own among miners and adventurers. The novel pairs northern adventure with a debate about what a woman may be.
16054-the-palace-of-darkened-windows:
An Eastern romance by Mary Hastings Bradley, author of The Favor of Kings, issued by D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1914. Edmund Frederick supplied the pictures. A frontispiece warns a girl in chapter four: there is no way out for her. Bradley dedicates the book to her husband. The palace of darkened windows holds the tale's mystery.

An eavesdropper, a captain's call, and a sorry quest lead within the palace walls. A girl in the bazaars, Billy's doubts, and a midnight visitor raise the stakes. A desperate game, a maid and a message, and a flight over the garden wall follow, with a girl from the harem and a rose room. The novel thrills as an Eastern adventure: veils, walls, and a rescue against the odds.
16398-what-necessity-knows:
L. Dougall's What Necessity Knows, published in New York by Longmans, Green in 1893 and inscribed to her brother John Redpath Dougall, draws on a childhood tradition of religious excitement. Its preface recalls the Millerite or Adventist stir of 1843. In one place a little band in white robes climbed a hill expecting the Second Advent. They then returned to be the laughing stock of neighbors. A child heard the tale as eccentricity, yet felt awe and pathos.

Dougall sets that picturesque event among gain-getting, market-driven neighbors, letting faith and commerce collide. The novel that follows tests belief, love, and necessity in a small community. Readers who like Victorian Canadian fiction will find a thoughtful, unusual story.
16729-lay-sermons-addresses-and-reviews:
Thomas Henry Huxley gathered these lay sermons, addresses, and reviews in 1870, issued by Macmillan in London. A prefatory letter to his friend Tyndall explains why the book has no formal dedication or preface. A grand lodge in front of cottages would look wrong. A full defense of old papers would mean writing a new one. The papers span years of his public work.

Huxley speaks as a man of science to a lay crowd, on nature, education, and the claims of faith and fact. His tone is bold, clear, and combative, with wit to match. The book gives a fine entry to Victorian science in public debate, and it shows Huxley as teacher, critic, and defender of free inquiry.
1750-laws:
Three old men walking the roads of Crete talk about founding a city from scratch, and the talk grows into Plato's longest work. Three old men — an Athenian, a Spartan, and a Cretan — walk and talk about founding a new city. They lay down its laws in detail: education, marriage, property, courts, and the worship of the gods.

Unlike the Republic, which imagines rule by philosophers, the Laws settles for second best: written law, mixed rule, and citizens trained by habit. Its genuineness is backed by Aristotle's many citations of it. Readers will find Plato at his most practical here, and also his most severe, as he tries to build a city that could actually stand.
1875-painted-windows:
Elia W. Peattie's Painted Windows invites the reader into the chamber of memory, to lift eyes to windows where figures and scenes of childhood appear. Peattie writes of her own past with kindly eyes, hoping that long wished-for visions of the reader's own will rise beside them.

The sketches that follow move through storms that carry the writer beyond excitement into exultation, where conceit and sulkiness die and she finds herself alive and loved. Peattie's prose is warm and reflective, and the book works as a memoir in fragments, each window lit by a moment that shaped a life.
18859-cross-purposes-and-the-shadows:
George MacDonald gathered two fairy tales in this volume: Cross Purposes and The Shadows. The first opens in Fairyland, where the queen, bored by her too-well-behaved subjects, longs for a mortal or two at court. Her courtier Peaseblossom offers to fetch a girl, opening the road before her and closing it behind her.

Both tales use fairy magic to test human character, with children and ordinary folk caught in enchantments that reveal their true selves. MacDonald's stories mix wonder with moral reflection, in the Victorian fairy-tale manner. Readers get two gentle, imaginative tales, suitable for reading aloud, from a writer much admired by later fantasy authors.
1922-deirdre-of-the-sorrows:
J. M. Synge's Deirdre of the Sorrows, his last play, retells the Irish legend of Deirdre. She is the girl fated to bring ruin to kings, and Naisi is the lover she runs away with. The persons of the play include Lavarcham, Deirdre's nurse, and Owen, a servant, and the acts move from Deirdre's youth to her flight and return.

Deirdre, grown to a queen, tells Naisi how she heard a voice singing in the woods at full moon, gathered up her skirts and ran on a little path she had found. Synge writes the legend in prose of great beauty, and the play's tragedy lies in its knowledge: Deirdre sees her fate clearly and walks toward it anyway.
19901-the-castle-of-the-shadows:
Mrs. C. N. Williamson wrote The Castle of the Shadows as a romance of Italy. Afternoon sunshine pours over its opening scene in a valley. Wooded hills shut the valley in on either side. Their rugged heads stay gilded while their shoulders fall into shadow. A girl's hair burns gold in that light. Two men watch her, and the watching matters. Williamson builds desire out of landscape.

The Williamsons' romances sold travel and love in one package. A castle of shadows promises secrets, pursuit, and a hidden past. Italian scenery does half their storytelling work. This novel follows their proven, popular pattern. Readers got a tour and a courtship together. It is Edwardian romance at full polish.
20447-the-works-of-robert-g-ingersoll-vo:
Robert G. Ingersoll was America's most famous lecturer against orthodox religion, and this eighth volume of his works gathers his interviews. Reporters asked him about the Bible, the church, and the afterlife. He answered in the plain, bold style that filled halls across the country.

Ingersoll says he regards the Bible, above all the Old Testament, as he does most other ancient books. In it he finds some truth, a great deal of error, considerable barbarism, and a most plentiful lack of good sense. The interviews preserve his wit and his case for free thought.
21657-deep-furrows:
Hopkins Moorhouse tells how prairie farmers built co-operatives in Deep Furrows, copyrighted in Canada in 1918. Wheatlands spread to the skyline around the Qu'Appelle trail in October 1901. A rider seems to hang still in the vast landscape as the tale opens.

The trail forks through the Qu'Appelle valley toward the Pheasant Hills and Fishing Lakes. Moorhouse frames the history as a tale of pioneer trails and hard fights. Farmers of western Canada won great feats in co-operation along those roads. Verse by E. Pauline Johnson, on the legend of Qu'Appelle, sets the book's elegiac tone.
22237-messages-from-the-epistle-to-the-h:
Messages from the Epistle to the Hebrews gathers the large spiritual lessons of that New Testament letter. The writer refuses two temptations at the start. He will not argue about who wrote Hebrews, and he will not expound it verse by verse in a few short chapters. Instead he takes the epistle as it stands, somewhat as a whole.

From it he draws conspicuous messages, as he calls them, of the Word that lives and abides forever. Faith, priesthood, sacrifice, and endurance are the letter's great themes. The book is devotional rather than critical, meant for Bible readers at home. It shows the preaching style that treated Hebrews as a storehouse of comfort for tired churches.
2705-sally-dows:
Bret Harte opens Sally Dows with a prologue on the last gun at Snake River, where a dewy country lane turns by noon into a scene of war's aftermath. The title story follows Sally herself, with the conspiracy of Mrs. Bunker and the transformation of Buckeye Camp.

Their uncle from California brings eastern money and western manners into collision. Harte writes of post war California with his usual mix of romance and irony, and Sally stands as one of his strongest heroines. The volume shows Harte's later craft, compact, humane, and quietly surprising.
27805-the-wind-in-the-willows:
Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows appears here in the 1913 Scribner's edition, illustrated by Paul Bransom, after a 1908 copyright. The story begins with Mole spring-cleaning his little home, then flinging down his brush and bolting out into spring.

Mole meets Rat, Badger, and the incorrigible Toad, and the chapters move from the river bank and the open road through the wild wood to Toad's adventures and the return of Ulysses. Gentle, funny, and lyrical, the book has become a classic of children's literature and of English pastoral imagination.
28763-imaginary-interviews:
William Dean Howells wrote this 1910 book of essays framed as conversations that never happened. The imaginary interviews take up New York life, Italian opera, vaudeville, magazines, travel, and the habits of rich and poor city folk. Extra essays treat autumn, letter writing, and advice from literary age to literary youth. Harper and Brothers published it in New York and London.

Howells uses the interview form to air opinions lightly: a niece advises her uncle on writing, a home-comer sizes up New York, and a grandfather talks about reading. The pieces are witty rather than angry, and they show a leading American novelist commenting on his own changing country. The book suits readers who like social observation done with humor and a light hand.
289-the-wind-in-the-willows:
Mole, tired of spring cleaning, meets Rat on the river bank and never looks back. Kenneth Grahame's Wind in the Willows follows Mole, Rat, Badger, and the reckless Toad through woods, roads, and river days. Toad's motorcar mania lands him in prison and his home in weasel hands.

Chapters like Dulce Domum, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, and Wayfarers All mix comedy with wonder. The animals' friendship, food, and fights feel deeply English and deeply human. Grahame wrote the tales for his son, and they grew into a classic. The book endures as a children's masterpiece.
29505-suggestions-to-the-jews:
Written by a Jew and printed in London by John Wertheimer and Company, this pamphlet offers suggestions to the Jews for improvement in reference to their charities, education, and general government. Its argument grows from hope and fear, from a sense of the community's own best interests and those of its posterity. Honor and reputation, the author says, must guide reform from within.

The pamphlet speaks as an insider to insiders, urging better organization of charity, schooling, and communal rule. Its tone is earnest and practical, not polemical. Students of Anglo-Jewish history will find a rare, early nineteenth-century voice on communal self-improvement, written before emancipation debates reshaped the question.
30193-east-of-the-shadows:
Mrs. Hubert Barclay, Edith Noël Barclay, sets a novel of love and choice in England, published at Toronto by Hodder and Stoughton in 1913. Chapters named Philippa, Phil, the stranger, Francis, Isabella, Doctor Gale, and indecision lead to the heart of Bessmoor, a square in the patchwork, the major's visit, and violets. Progress, threads, ropes of gossamer, and revelation follow, with hopes for the future, Isabella's point of view, and Marion speaking her mind.

The opening sends a train out of a terminus, its porter slamming a door, its engine snorting, its cars gliding through a maze of buildings. Philippa, courteous though coy and gentle though retired, carries the story's center, in the words of Crabbe quoted at her chapter head. Halcyon days, bitter-sweet hours, poor Rip, friendship, and content close a tale of hearts tested and settled.
31088-taxonomy-and-distribution-of-some-:
James S. Findley's 1955 paper tidies the taxonomy and ranges of several American shrews, published as volume 7, number 14 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. Two Ohio specimens long listed as the common cinereous shrew prove, on small size, short tails, and tooth form, to belong to the subspecies ohionensis. That pushes its known range about seventy miles south to Milford Center.

A Veracruz shrew earlier assigned to a Texas form is likewise shown to be Cryptotis micrura on comparison with specimens from northern Veracruz and southern Tamaulipas. Short and specimen-based, the paper shows museum taxonomy at work, correcting names one skin and skull at a time.
31715-a-prince-of-good-fellows:
Robert Barr's Prince of Good Fellows, illustrated by Edmund J. Sullivan, was published at New York by McClure, Phillips, and Company in May 1902, with copyright in 1901 and 1902. Its eleven stories follow a king through a round of adventures, and their titles tell the course: the king intervenes, dines, keeps a tryst, and investigates. Then come the king's gold, the king a-begging, and the king's visit.

The king explores, drinks, sails, and at last weds, closing a sequence of courtly comedy and adventure. Barr's stories are light, gallant, and good-humored, and they show a prince who meets the world on its own terms.
32116-when-the-cock-crows:
Waldron Baily's adventure novel, published in New York by the Bedford Publishing Company in 1918 with drawings by G. W. Gage, is a coastal tale built around a man named Ichabod. Baily had earlier written Heart of the Blue Ridge and The Homeward Trail. He dedicated this book to Josephus Daniels, praised for courage, determination, and achievement in a great crisis. Its contents promise island life, storms, and a hero's slow awakening.

The chapters run from Ichabod's Island and Among the Breakers, through a new calamity, a prisoner of morphia, and a hunt for a clue, to stormbound days and eyes from the deep. Later chapters give the awakening of Ichabod, scenes among fisherfolk, Garnet the hero, and an episode adrift with a madman, before a coming-out party closes the list. Readers get a period sea-coast romance, mixing mystery, danger, and a community bound to the water.
32968-the-expositor-s-bible-the-epistle-:
Thomas Charles Edwards, principal of the University College of Wales, wrote this volume on the Epistle to the Hebrews for the Expositor's Bible series, edited by W. Robertson Nicoll and published in London in 1904. Edwards works through the letter passage by passage, explaining its argument about Christ, priesthood, sacrifice, and faith for preachers and general readers rather than for specialists alone.

The commentary treats Hebrews as a careful, sustained piece of reasoning, not a loose set of sayings, and it tries to show how each part serves the whole. Edwards's tone is learned but pastoral, aiming to help a reader preach or study the text with confidence. As a work of Edwardian biblical exposition, it remains a clear guide to one of the New Testament's hardest letters.
32997-the-style-book-of-the-detroit-news:
The Style Book of the Detroit News gathers the rules that governed writing and editing at one of Michigan's leading papers. Its editor drew on government and university style books and on standard works on newspaper writing, with permission to adapt a digest of New York libel law to Michigan. Inscriptions on the newspaper's building, written by Professor Fred N. Scott of Michigan, appear in boxes.

The book also records the paper's own history, founded by James Edmund Scripps in 1873, with a Sunday edition from 1884. As a style book, it shows what editors valued: clear spelling, consistent usage, and care with law and libel. For journalists and historians of the press, it is a compact window on how a great city daily taught its staff to write fairly and well.
33112-shapes-and-shadows:
Madison Cawein's Shapes and Shadows gathers poems that move from nature and memory to love, art, and the nation's wars. Its contents run from The Evanescent Beautiful and August through The Higher Brotherhood, Gramarye, and Dreams. They go on to The Old House, The Rock, and Rain, then on to Standing-Stone Creek, The Moonmen, and The Old Man Dreams. Later poems include Tristram and Isolt, Dusk in the Woods, At the Ferry, and a southern girl and a daughter of the states.

An opening patriotic poem under the stars and stripes, urging sons to uphold the name their fathers blazoned, shows Cawein's public voice beside his private lyrics. The collection's dedication speaks of bards of old and the flame that fell on them, and Cawein's own verse aims for musical beauty and feeling. It is a representative volume from a Kentucky poet once widely read.
4554-lovers-vows:
Mrs. Inchbald adapted this play in five acts from the German of Kotzebue, and it is set in Germany over a single day. The action moves between a small inn, a cottage, a castle, and a prison tower, following Baron Wildenhaim, Count Cassel, Anhalt, Frederick, and the women around them, Agatha Firburg and Amelia Wildenhaim. A prologue and epilogue frame the drama, which was written for the stage with named actors in mind.

At its heart lies a story of seduction, family duty, and forgiveness, as old wrongs surface and young lovers press their claims. Inchbald keeps the pace brisk, shifting scenes between high road, cottage room, and castle chamber. Readers get a lively late Georgian drama about honour, rank, and second chances, best read aloud or imagined on stage, where each act tightens the knot before it is cut.
4594-home-lights-and-shadows:
T. S. Arthur published Home Lights and Shadows at New York in 1853, gathering short domestic sketches under one moral idea. His preface says that love makes the home-lights and selfishness the shadows, and that few people never darken, for a time, the homes that should grow bright at their coming. The contents include Rights and Wrongs, The Humbled Pharisee, and Romance and Reality. They go on to Both to Blame, The Mother's Promise, The Two Husbands, and Visiting as Neighbors.

Later sketches cover a dollar on the conscience, helping the poor, following the fashions, and making a sensation, among other homely cases. Each piece is short, plain, and aimed at conduct in family life. Readers get a typical mid-century American gift book of moral tales, easy to dip into story by story. It is a clear window into what Victorian households were taught to praise and to avoid.
4766-windows:
John Galsworthy wrote Windows as a play in the fifth series of his plays, set in Geoffrey March's house at Highgate in springtime. Its persons include Geoffrey March, his wife Joan, and their children Mary and Johnny. Their cook, Mr. Bly, their window cleaner, and his daughter Faith Bly also appear, with Blunter, a strange young man, and Mr. Barnadas.

Act one opens on a Thursday morning in the dining-room after breakfast. Act two follows a fortnight later after lunch, and act three the same day after dinner. The dining-room opens through French windows onto a garden that seems infinite, till side walls show it finite at the far end, where acacias and sumachs screen another house. French and other windows form all the outer wall. Readers get a tense Galsworthy play about a household, a stranger, and what windows reveal and hide.
5654-what-every-woman-knows:
James M. Barrie wrote What Every Woman Knows as a comedy opening in a little Scotch room, where James Wylie is about to move on the draughtboard amid an awful silence befitting the occasion. With his hand poised, since touching a piece means playing it, James raises his red head to read his father Alick's face. Alick pretends panic lest James make this move, then is caught in unholy ecstasy as James grins.

The play follows Maggie Wylie and John Shand, asking what a woman knows and what a man owes her wit. Barrie writes Scottish family comedy with tenderness. Readers get a beloved stage comedy about marriage, ambition, and the quiet power behind success.
5895-the-honor-of-the-big-snows:
James Oliver Curwood opens The Honor of the Big Snows at a bedside in the north woods, where a woman whispers to John that she hears music. Her white, thin hand lifts weakly to the rough face of the man kneeling beside her bed. Her great dark eyes grow luminously bright for a moment. She whispers again that she hears music. A sigh follows, and the chapter, called The Music, sets the novel's tone.

The tale follows a story of the Canadian snow country, where honor, love, and survival are tested by cold and distance. Curwood writes with vivid northern atmosphere, favoring emotion and adventure over subtlety. The book suits readers of wilderness romance, and fans of Curwood's tales of Mounties, trappers, and the big snows themselves.
7807-georgina-of-the-rainbows:
Annie Fellows Johnston's Georgiana of the Rainbows, set at old Cape Cod, follows a girl through playmate mothers, town criers, green stairs, pirate steps, and spend-the-day guests. A telegram takes Barby away, a birthday prism shines, moving pictures flicker, and an old rifle gives up its secret.

Later chapters bring buried treasure, a narrow escape, a storm, dunes, a liniment wagon, a wild-cat woman, rainbow games, and light dawning for Uncle Darcy. Dedicated to a little goddaughter, Anne Elizabeth, the book mixes seaside adventure with family feeling and a child's bright fancy.
8058-the-bible-king-james-version-book-5:
Hebrews opens without a greeting, arguing that God, who once spoke through prophets, has now spoken through his Son, heir of all things and brightness of God's glory. The letter presents Jesus as greater than angels, greater than Moses, and the true high priest who offers himself once for all. Its readers, tempted to drift back, are urged to hold fast, warned against falling away, and cheered by the roll of faith in chapter eleven.

Hebrews is the New Testament's most sustained piece of theology, weaving the Old Testament sacrificial system into an argument for Christ. Its language is elevated and its reasoning intricate. In the King James Version, its phrases about faith as the substance of things hoped for have become part of English devotion, and the letter remains essential for understanding early Christian thought.
8285-the-world-english-bible-web-hebrews:
Hebrews is a sermon more than a letter, written to Jewish Christians tempted to drift back to old ways. Its unknown author argues that Jesus surpasses angels, Moses, and the high priests, and that his single sacrifice replaces the repeated offerings of the temple. Long chains of Old Testament quotations build the case, step by step.

The famous chapter on faith then marches through Abel, Abraham, Moses, and others who trusted without seeing the promise fulfilled. It closes with plain calls to endure hardship and care for one another. Hebrews rewards slow reading: dense, poetic, and argued like a lawyer's brief for staying the course.
8846-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Hebrews, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens with God, who in ancient days spoke to forefathers in many distinct messages and by various methods through the prophets. Speaking at the end of these days through a Son, predestined Lord of the universe, through whom he made the ages. The Son brightly reflects God's glory, is the exact representation of his being, upholds the universe by his powerful word. And, after securing purification from sin, sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.

Superior to angels by the name he inherits, the Son becomes the letter's centre. Hebrews argues from priesthood, sacrifice, and covenant that Christ fulfils and surpasses the old order. Weymouth's plain version helps readers follow the letter's long, intricate argument. Hebrews is the New Testament's most theological book, and this volume gives it whole, in modern English that keeps its grandeur without its archaisms.
9314-the-calling-of-dan-matthews:
Harold Bell Wright wrote this novel in 1909 about Dan Matthews, a young minister finding his calling. The story opens in Corinth, with Hope Farwell's ministry, the home of the Ally, and a great day in town. Dan sees the other side, faces tragedy, and learns to save a life, not just preach about one.

Chapters on fishing, common ground, and a laborer and his hire carry Dan from pulpit pride to humble service. Wright, famed for The Shepherd of the Hills, writes plainly and warmly. The novel remains a popular tale of faith tested by real work and real people.
9509-southern-lights-and-shadows:
Southern Lights and Shadows, a Harper's collection from 1907, gathers short tales of the American South. William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited the set, with tales by Grace MacGowan Cooke, Abby Meguire Roach, and Alice MacGowan. The Capture of Andy Proudfoot opens, as a woodsman stalks a man through pine woods. Other tales range from piny woods to mammy's kitchen and a snipe hunt.

Stories include Pap Overholt, The Level of Fortune, and The Courtship of Colonel Bill, each with a Southern voice and scene. Humor, danger, and local color mix in equal parts. A reader gets a vivid sampler of Southern short fiction, told by writers who knew the region's speech and soil.
a-daughter-of-the-snows: Jack London tells of Frona Welse, a daughter of the snows in gold rush Alaska. The novel opens aboard a steamer, where Frona hurries ashore toward a big log house among the pines. Gold rushers crowd the country, and Frona meets their world with spirit and independence. London writes a northern tale of love, courage, and the claims of civilization.
a-merry-dialogue-declaringe-the-properti: Desiderius Erasmus writes a merry dialogue declaring the properties of shrewd shrews and honest wives. Translated into English in 1557, the dialogue is pleasant and profitable in the author's manner. Erasmus, the famous clerk of Rotterdam, stages a debate on marriage. The old spelling of the text is preserved for modern readers.
britannica-1911-agrarian-laws:
Agrarian Laws concern the public land of ancient Rome. Ager publicus was land won by conquest. Republic principle barred free gifts of state property. The people's consent was needed for any disposal. Land could be leased for state revenue instead. Dues were paid by those occupying it. Land could also be assigned to poor citizens. Assignment ended state ownership of the plot. Colonies planted garrisons and relieved poverty at once. Roman speakers linked agrarian law with colonization closely.

Tenure conditions are traced through laws. The Lex Agraria of 111 B.C. reveals African practice. Tax farmers collected dues from possessors there. Caps protected occupiers from overcharging by farmers. Later emperors tried reclaiming unassigned oddments of land. Domitian finally recognized such holdings as private property. The huge entry runs from early Republic to Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptismal-vow:
Baptismal vows are the popular name for renunciations made by an adult just before baptism, or by sponsors for infants. They lack the theological weight of vows properly so called. The Roman Ritual asks three questions, each pressing whether the person renounces Satan, his works, and his pomps. To each, the person or sponsor answers, 'I do renounce.'

The practice reaches back to organized Christian worship's beginnings, upheld by Tertullian and St Basil as venerable tradition. Basil traces it to the Apostles, though Scripture does not explicitly warrant it. The Apostolic Constitutions give a fuller form, renouncing Satan, his works, pomps, worship, angels, and inventions. The candidate then turns east, toward light, and pledges himself to Christ, to be ruled by his precepts. Renewal of these promises is widespread at missions, First Communions, and Confirmations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-to-th:
The Epistle to the Hebrews is treated under argument, doctrine, style, readers, author, circumstances, and importance. In the oldest Greek manuscripts it follows the letters to the churches and precedes the pastoral letters. Later copies place it last among Paul's epistles. It opens without Paul's usual introduction, announcing the superiority of the Son's revelation over the prophets'.

From Scripture it proves the New Covenant's superiority over the Old. The Son stands above angels as mediators of the Old Covenant, above Moses and Joshua as its founders, and Christ's priesthood after Melchisedech above the Levitical priesthood after Aaron. Doctrinal statements are broken again and again by practical exhortations to hold fast to the faith and not slip back into Mosaic worship. The second part repeats calls to steadfast faith and Christian living, closing with personal remarks and a greeting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th:
This long article covers Jewish history from the return from Babylonian exile onward. Before that return, the people were called Israelites. From 538 BC they took the name Jews. A separate article treats Judaism as a religious communion, while this one follows the people's political and social story.

The story is told in periods shaped by ruling powers. It opens with Persian suzerainty, when Cyrus let the exiles return to Juda in 538 BC. Later periods follow Greek, Roman, and later rulers, tracing how Jewish life survived conquest, dispersion, and changing empires. Readers get a full chronological frame for two thousand years of history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penal-laws:
The penal laws were the statutes that squeezed Catholic life in English-speaking lands after the Reformation. This long Catholic Encyclopedia survey takes England, Scotland, Ireland, and the American colonies in turn. In England, sovereigns and parliaments from Elizabeth to George III piled up measures that barred Catholic worship, stripped civil rights, and put estates and sometimes lives at the mercy of informers.

No code ever gathered the laws into one system, since each measure answered a political moment. The survey groups them by their targets: worship itself, refusal to conform, refusal of the Oath of Supremacy and the Test Acts, and the holding of land. It follows the same pattern abroad, showing how Scotland, Ireland, and the colonies each built their own version of exclusion before relief slowly arrived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-laws:
Poor Laws are the legal enactments made in many countries at many periods for the relief of destitution and sickness among the poor. In England the system is the most comprehensive. It is the fruit of nearly four centuries of experiment. It was still under review after the Royal Commission on the Poor Laws reported in 1909. That commission sat three years, heard over 1,300 witnesses, and made over 800 visits.

The commission's 1,250-page report split between a majority of fourteen and a minority of four, and rival associations formed to push each side's recommendations. The entry contrasts England with Denmark. In Denmark officials take trouble to keep deserving people from becoming paupers through misfortune or illness. Applicants there may seek advice, a loan, or a gift. Yet relief there carries penalties England would not tolerate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priory-of-sai:
The Priory of Saint Andrews was one of Scotland's great religious houses and the country's metropolitan church ere the Reformation.  Angus, King of the Picts from 735 to 747, stands as its first founder, giving Bishop Regulus, bringer to Scotland of St Andrew's relics, meadows, fields, and other goods. From the start, perhaps, Culdees ran the church and held the right to elect the bishop.

In 1144, at King Alexander I's request, Scone's Prior Robert became St Andrews' bishop. Alexander, for his many gifts, may be called the priory's second founder. Robert brought brother canons regular and settled them in the priory. Canons and Culdees served side by side for a time. By the pope's 1147 order the Culdees, who had refused the choice to turn canons, lost their place, and the canons gained all their rights. From then until the Reformation the canons formed the Cathedral Chapter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-brehon-la:
Ireland's native law, administered down to near the middle of the seventeenth century, is the subject of this substantial entry. Its name comes from breitheamh, the Irish word for a judge. English conquest finally displaced it among the native Irish, but a rich body of law tracts survived in a difficult, highly technical tongue.

Two scholars unlocked them: Eugene O'Curry and John O'Donovan, the first since Duald Mac Firbis, murdered in 1670, to master the language. Working in Dublin, London, and Oxford libraries, O'Curry transcribed eight volumes totalling 2,906 pages and O'Donovan nine more with 2,491. Courts, contracts, land, kinship, and penalties emerge from their labours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
St Andrews began in an association of learned churchmen formed in 1410, among them Laurence of Lindores, Abbot of Scone, Richard Cornwall, Archdeacon of Lothian, and William Stephen, later Archbishop of Dunblane. They offered lectures in divinity, logic, philosophy, and canon and civil law. In 1411 Bishop Henry Wardlaw granted a charter of privilege and asked the antipope Benedict XIII, whose legate he was, for a founding bull, backing the claims Scotland supported.

The bull came in 1413 and won confirmation by royal charter from James I in 1532. In 1911 the foundation's five-hundredth anniversary was celebrated. The university comprised three colleges: St Salvator's, founded in 1450 by Bishop James Kennedy, with St Leonard's and St Mary's following. The entry traces their growth, their Reformation troubles, and their union into the modern university.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vows:
A vow is defined as a promise made to God, binding in a way a simple resolution, a present purpose about the future, is not. Between people a promise pledges faith, inviting trust and dependence, and breaking it destroys mutual confidence, which natural law condemns shaking. With God the reasoning differs: no one can deceive God about present intention, and he knows whether the maker will persevere.

What makes a vow distinctive is offering God not only a present thing or action but a future action and perseverance in fulfilling it. Changing purpose afterward disrespects God like taking back a dedicated gift, sacrilege in the widest sense. Later sections distinguish simple and solemn vows, public and private vows, and the vows of religion, placing material solemnity, with Vasquez, Sanchez. Others, in surrender followed by irrevocable acceptance, and treating dispensation, commutation, and the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-euseb:
William Eusebius Andrews was an English Catholic pressman who founded paper after paper for the Catholic cause. Born at Norwich in 1773 to convert parents of humble station, he died in London in 1837. He apprenticed at the Norfolk Chronicle, rose to edit it from 1799 to 1813, then moved to London to push Catholic rights through print. In July 1813 he launched the Orthodox Journal and Catholic Monthly Intelligencer with Bishop Milner's aid.

Money troubles dogged him: the Orthodox Journal halted in 1820, the Glasgow Catholic Vindicator lasted a year, the Catholic Advocate nine months, and the People's Advocate seven weeks. Later ventures included the Truth Teller of 1824, famed for hammering O'Connell, and the Penny Orthodox Journal of 1832. His New York Truth Teller of 1825, the city's first Catholic paper, bore his firm's imprint on its first six issues. His liberty society spread nearly five hundred thousand tracts in just over a year.
deirdre-of-the-sorrows:
J M Synge wrote Deirdre of the Sorrows in three acts from the Irish legend of Deirdre and the sons of Usna, leaving the play nearly finished at his early death. Lavarcham's house on Slieve Fuadh opens the action, with a half-finished tapestry on the frame. King Conchubor raised Deirdre in seclusion to be his own bride; she chose Naisi instead.

Exile in Scotland, Fergus's treacherous safe-conduct, and the return to Emain Macha drive the tragedy. A timid woman, Deirdre taunts, should not frighten the sons of Usna away from a kingly life. Synge's Hiberno-English dialogue gives the old tale a peasant music no translation had found. The Abbey Theatre staged it in 1910 with his fiancee as Deirdre.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CBS-TVNewsSpeci:
In June 1967 CBS News did something unusual: it put the Warren Report on trial on television. This transcript holds the fourth and final installment of the CBS News Inquiry into the report, broadcast June 28, 1967.

Walter Cronkite anchored, with Dan Rather, Eric Sevareid, and KRLD-TV's Eddie Barker, who had covered Dallas on the day of the assassination. The series examined the evidence and, in the end, largely upheld the Warren Commission's findings, a verdict that angered the report's growing body of critics. The transcript preserves broadcast journalism's most serious early reckoning with the case.
home-lights-and-shadows:
T. S. Arthur published Home Lights and Shadows in New York in 1853, a volume of domestic tales. His preface gives the book's doctrine in one line of thought. Love makes the home-lights, and selfishness makes the shadows. Every story tests some household against that rule.

Rights and Wrongs opens the collection with Mrs. Uhler, who will not honour and obey. Other tales include The Humbled Pharisee, The Mother's Promise, and The Two Husbands. A Dollar on the Conscience and Following the Fashions treat money and vanity. Arthur writes for the parlour, with scenes of visits, portraits, and poor relations. The tales are short, pointed, and openly moral. They ask readers to confess their own selfishness as the first step toward brighter homes.
laws:
Plato's Laws is his longest and latest dialogue, translated here by Benjamin Jowett. Jowett's introduction first defends the work as truly Plato's. Aristotle cites it more than twenty times, he notes.

Three older men walk and talk about how a city should be ruled. They design laws for a new colony in careful detail. Education, property, religion, and crime all receive rules. The tone is graver than in Plato's earlier dialogues. Readers find here his final, practical vision of a well-ordered state. An Athenian stranger leads the discussion through most books. Crete's mountains form the walking setting for their talk.
lay-sermons-addresses-and-reviews:
Thomas Henry Huxley collected his Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews in 1870. Macmillan published the volume in London. A prefatory letter to his friend Tyndall opens the book.

Huxley explains that he wanted both a dedication and a preface. He links the book to Tyndall as his oldest scientific ally. The essays defend science, evolution, and free inquiry in plain terms. He writes as a preacher of nature rather than of church doctrine. The collection shows why crowds called him Darwin's bulldog. The very title claims a pulpit for science. Huxley's plain style made complex ideas feel urgent and clear.
lovers-vows:
Lovers' Vows is a play in five acts by August von Kotzebue. Mrs. Inchbald translated and adapted it from the German. The scenes shift between a cottage, a castle, and a prison tower. Baron Wildenhaim, Count Cassel, and the tutor Anhalt lead the cast.

The play tells of Frederick, a poor soldier who comes home seeking help. His mother lives in the cottage, hiding a sorrowful secret. Love, shame, and forgiveness drive the story to its close. English readers know this play from Jane Austen's Mansfield Park. There, staging it causes a famous household scandal. It remains a prime sample of the sentimental German drama.
painted-windows:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie opens Painted Windows with an invitation. Come into the chamber of memory, she writes. Lift your eyes to the painted windows there. Figures and scenes of childhood appear in them. Six chapters follow: Night, Solitude, Friendship, Fame, Remorse, and Travel. The book is a memoir arranged by the lights memory shines through.

Night argues that memory has compensations youth lacks. Old pleasures are less breathless than young ones. They are delicate and fine instead. Few of us would exchange our memories for another's. They have become part of our personality. Peattie can run over her childhood incidents like chapters. She takes them out at night, or on long journeys, and reads them again.
podcast-joerogan-o_R1zoY9kWs:
Jimmy Corsetti, the YouTuber behind the Bright Insight channel, brings his Atlantis theory to the Joe Rogan Experience in this segment. Corsetti argues that Plato's lost city was real. He points to a strange round formation in the Sahara desert as its likely site.

Corsetti walks through Plato's description and matches it against the Richat Structure in Mauritania. He talks about floods, old maps, and why he thinks experts dismiss the idea too fast. Rogan asks hard questions about dates and proof. The segment gives the Atlantis hunt a modern, online face and a clear claim to judge.
podcast-joerogan-wt2sI8OdmWs:
Money coach Caleb Hammer joins Joe Rogan for episode 2509. Hammer audits strangers' finances on his hit online show. He shows guests their debts and habits in blunt charts.

Rogan asks how so many people fall so deep into debt. Hammer blames cards, car loans, and daily spending leaks. He lays out the fixes he gives on his show. The episode is dollars and sense in plain talk. Listeners in debt get both a warning and a path, from a man who reads budgets for a living. Tough love is the whole method on display.
podcast-tuckercarlson-K_czibJylWs:
Tucker Carlson opens the occult itself as this episode's subject. He covers Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition, and the Antichrist's newest form as his material presents it. He also gives practical instruction on avoiding the mark of the beast described in Revelation. The program reads current events through the end-times text directly.

Carlson's recent work has moved steadily toward treating politics as a spiritual conflict with named combatants, and this episode states that reading at full length. His audience hears prophecy applied to headlines without apology. Others will find the framework alien, which is itself a reason the recording matters. It documents, in a leading broadcaster's own words, a large public interpreting the news through occult categories. Those categories were once left to late-night radio.
reviews:
Oscar Wilde's newspaper reviews are gathered here, in an edition of 1908 from Methuen, seen through the press by Robert Ross. Ross, who managed Wilde's literary and dramatic property after his death, dedicates the book to Mrs. Carew. He thanks her for a kindness that annulled eight years of disappointments in that work.

The first review, from the Pall Mall Gazette of March 7, 1885, treats a cookbook called Dinners and Dishes. Wilde jokes that no man can live a day without poetry, yet none can live without eating either. Cookery is an art, he insists, and he praises the book's brevity and its lack of pictures of legs of mutton.
sally-dows:
Bret Harte wrote Sally Dows, a gathering that also holds The Conspiracy of Mrs. Bunker, The Transformation of Buckeye Camp, and Their Uncle from California. The title tale opens with a prologue headed The Last Gun at Snake River. A cool, dewy country lane at summer morning, marked only by wagon tracks and the faint prints of a crossing fox or coon. By high noon it is crushed and trampled out of all likeness to its grace. Gun-carriages, caissons, and the hoofs of crowding cavalry have cut and shredded its grassy borders under a cloud of dust.

Scattered muskets, gear, knapsacks, caps, and clothing litter the ruined way, with broken wagons thrown into the ditch. For two hours the greater part of an army corps has passed and repassed, always with faces turned eagerly toward an open slope on the right. Yet nothing is to be seen there.
some-private-views: James Payn wrote Some Private Views. A new edition came out in 1881. Chatto and Windus of Piccadilly, London, printed it. Payn also wrote High Spirits and A Confidential Agent. He gives this book to his friend Horace N. Pym. The contents group pieces from the Nineteenth Century review. The Midway Inn and The Critic on the Hearth stand there. Sham Admiration in Literature appears as well. Pieces from the Times treat hotels and servants. Whist-players, kin, and wet holidays fill out the list.
southern-lights-and-shadows:
William Dean Howells and Henry Mills Alden edited Southern Lights and Shadows for Harper's Novelettes, dated 1907. The table of contents names Grace MacGowan Cooke's The Capture of Andy Proudfoot first. Tales by Abby Meguire Roach, Alice MacGowan, Mrs. B. F. Mayhew, and William L. Sheppard follow, with pieces on a snipe hunt, the courtship of Colonel Bill, and the balance of power near the end.

Cooke's tale opens in the woods. A dry branch snaps under Kerry's foot with the crack of a toy pistol, and he swears by rote and stares with greed at a cave mouth just ahead. Kerry is a poor woodsman at best, the tale says, and now he stalks the greatest of all big game. The set of short Southern tales thus starts in a tense, sly key, with a hunter out of his depth.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-58-heb:
Hebrews , from the King James Bible, opens by recalling that God spoke in past times to the fathers by the prophets, in many portions and manners. In these last days, it says, he has spoken by his Son.

That Son is appointed heir of all things, and the worlds were made by him. He is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, upholding all things by his powerful word. After purging sins himself, he sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high. He is made better than the angels, with a more excellent name than theirs.
the-calling-of-dan-matthews: Harold Bell Wright wrote The Calling of Dan Matthews, dated 1909, with illustrations by Arthur I. Keller. Wright had also written The Shepherd of the Hills and That Printer of Udell's. He gave the book to William Williams, M.D. The chapters start with The Home of the Ally and A Revelation. A Great Day in Corinth and Who Are They come next. Hope Farwell's Ministry leads to the title chapter, The Calling of Dan Matthews. A Matter of Opinion and Reflections close the list shown.
the-honor-of-the-big-snows:
James Oliver Curwood wrote The Honor of the Big Snows, published in New York in 1911. He is named as the author of The Danger Trail and The Courage of Captain Plum. Chapter one, The Music, opens at a deathbed in a low-roofed cabin. A woman whispers to the man kneeling beside her that she hears music.

John Cummins hides his own eyes from her bright gaze and feels her thin hand quiver against his cheek. He tells his Melisse that the music is the pretty music in the skies, choking back sobs. She insists the music is real. Her flush fades as the pale glow of a northern sun fades before thickening snow, and Cummins reads the end in her face.
the-jews: Hilaire Belloc published this book with Constable of London in 1922. A second impression came the same year. He dedicated it to Miss Ruby Goldsmith. Only the publisher's front pages are present here. The argument itself does not appear. The front pages list his earlier works. Europe and the Faith stands among them. A Church Times notice calls that book a brilliant essay. It calls it his best book as well. The Old Road and The Stane Street follow. William Hyde drew the pictures for both.
the-palace-of-darkened-windows: Mary Hastings Bradley wrote The Palace of Darkened Windows. D. Appleton and Company published it in New York and London in 1914, with illustrations by Edmund Frederick. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list twenty-one chapters, from The Eavesdropper and At the Palace onward. A Girl in the Bazaars, The Girl from the Harem, and The Hidden Girl follow. Desert Magic closes the list of this eastern adventure.
the-singing-man-a-book-of-songs-and-shad: Josephine Preston Peabody published The Singing Man, a Book of Songs and Shadows, with Houghton Mifflin in 1911. The copyright names her as Josephine Peabody Marks. A note thanks magazine editors for reprint permission. The American Magazine, Scribner's, and The Atlantic Monthly are named. The pages shown give that note and the start of the contents only. The title poem comes first, at page three. The Trees, Rich Man Poor Man, and The Foundling follow. No poem text itself appears here.
the-willows:
Algernon Blackwood's Willows, dated 1907, is divided into five numbered sections. The opening travels down the Danube below Vienna, long before Budapest, where the river escapes its banks into a region of singular loneliness. For miles the country becomes swamp, covered by a vast sea of low willow-bushes that maps paint in fading blue and label Sümpfe, meaning marshes.

These willows never become trees. They stay humble bushes with rounded tops, swaying on slender stems, so that wind sends waves of leaves rolling like a green sea turning silvery underneath. The wandering river tears at sandy banks, builds new islands daily, and destroys them at flood-time. Blackwood's landscape writing makes the marsh itself feel moving and alive.
the-wind-in-the-willows:
Kenneth Grahame, author of The Golden Age and Dream Days, gives his animal tale twelve chapters, from The River Bank through Mr. Badger, Dulce Domum, and The Piper at the Gates of Dawn to The Return of Ulysses. Chapter one finds the Mole spring-cleaning his little home all morning, with brooms, dusters, ladders, and a pail of whitewash.

Dust fills Mole's throat and eyes, whitewash spots his black fur, and his back aches. Spring is moving in the air above and the earth below, filling even his dark house with divine discontent and longing. He flings down his brush, cries hang spring-cleaning, and bolts up his steep tunnel. His snout pops into sunlight and warm meadow grass, better by far than whitewashing.
the-world-english-bible-web-hebrews:
Hebrews occupies book fifty-eight in the World English Bible, written to believers needing endurance. God spoke in the past through prophets, the letter begins. Those messages came at many times and in various ways. Now God has spoken through his Son. The Son is heir of all things and maker of the worlds. His glory's radiance is described in exalted language.

After purifying sins, the Son sat down at God's right hand. He ranks far above the angels, the writer argues. Scripture citations from Psalms support the claim. No author signs this letter in the opening verses. Readers get a sermon-like case for Christ's supremacy and perseverance.
the-world-turned-upside-down-or-no-news-: An old chapbook called The World Turned Upside Down, or No News and Strange News, opens with a frontispiece verse. It promises pictures of trees and castles floating in the air, plus a man walking on his crown. Alphabet pages follow, in Roman and italic letters. A tailor riding a goose illustrates the fun. A closing rhyme contrasts a butcher killing a hog with a hare chasing a dog. Only these opening teaching pages appear in this record.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
Hebrews opens book 58 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. The writer says God spoke long ago through the prophets in many ways. Now, at the end of those days, God has spoken through a Son. That Son made the ages and holds up all things by his word.

After making a way to cleanse sin, the Son sat at God's right hand. He stands far above the angels, with a far greater name. Old texts are quoted to prove the point. Weymouth gives the dense thought in orderly modern prose. Readers meet a high view of Christ from the first lines.
what-every-woman-knows:
James M. Barrie wrote the play What Every Woman Knows. The first act opens on a Saturday night in the Wylie home in Scotland. Old Alick Wylie plays at draughts with his son James. Each man tries to trap the other into a bad move. The pauses grow so long that they may forget whose turn it is.

Barrie draws the plain back room with warmth and sly humor. Miss Wylie, the daughter, keeps a finer drawing room for callers. Family worship has sent the servant to bed, and the men play on. The comedy turns on a woman's quiet sway over the men around her.
what-necessity-knows:
L. Dougall published the novel What Necessity Knows with Longmans, Green in New York in 1893. Dougall gave the book to her brother John Redpath Dougall. Her preface explains one strange episode in the tale. It rests on tales of the Millerite excitement of 1843 in North America.

In one place, Dougall heard, a small band in white robes climbed a hill to await the end of the world. They came back down to face the laughs of neighbors. She wanted to treat their hope with awe, not scorn. The tale sets such faith beside gain, marriage, and plain town life. Handling that mix with care was her stated aim.
windows: The pages here list Galsworthy's plays by series and name Windows among the fifth series, but the play itself does not appear. John Galsworthy's fifth series also holds A Family Man and Loyalties. Earlier series named in the list include The Silver Box, Strife, Justice, and The Skin Game. Windows is shown with two act headings and no lines of dialogue. A first line in the record dates the set to 1922. Readers see where the play sits in Galsworthy's stage work, nothing more.
